title: The duty to act
subtitle: Actus reus and liability for omissions
objectives: State the general rule that the criminal law does not punish a failure to act, and explain why
Identify the six recognised situations in which a legal duty to act arises
Apply the duty categories to a new fact pattern and distinguish a duty situation from mere moral failure

leadingAuthorities.role: Duty arising from creating a dangerous situation

leadingAuthorities.citation: R v Stone and Dobinson [1977] QB 354
leadingAuthorities.role: Duty from voluntary assumption of care
Extends Miller to a shared duty of care between adults

leadingAuthorities.citation: Airedale NHS Trust v Bland [1993] AC 789
leadingAuthorities.role: Withdrawal of treatment as an omission, not an act

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can recite 'no liability for omissions' from memory. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the rule — this lesson is about spotting when it doesn't apply.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below is weighted towards application: expect fact patterns, not definitions.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take your time on the duty categories — the rest of the lesson assumes you can name all six without prompting.

overview.hook: A man drowns three feet from a crowded riverbank while a dozen people watch. Not one of them is guilty of anything. Change one fact — one of them pushed him in, twenty minutes earlier, by accident — and the law changes completely. This lesson is about where that line sits, and why it's drawn there at all.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 22 September 2026. This is a stable, long-settled area of common law; no legislative change is pending.

parts.heading: Why the law lets bystanders walk away
parts.voice: argumentative — states the strongest case for the rule, then complicates it
body: English law starts from a blunt principle: there is no general duty to rescue. You can watch a stranger drown, walk past a collapsed cyclist, or ignore a house fire next door, and commit no offence at all — however easy the rescue would have been, and however callous your reason for refusing.

This shocks most people on first hearing it. Civil law systems across Europe generally impose a 'Good Samaritan' duty; England and Wales does not. The usual justification isn't that omissions are harmless — clearly they aren't — but that turning every failure to help into a crime would police thought and character as much as conduct, and would require the law to rank whose moral duty came first when several bystanders stood by.

The rule has a name worth knowing precisely: there is no liability for a **pure omission**. The word 'pure' is doing real work — it marks the boundary this lesson exists to map, because the moment any of six recognised relationships is in play, 'pure' stops applying and a duty appears.

components.definition: A failure to act by someone under no recognised legal duty to the victim — the default position in English criminal law, which attracts no liability however serious the consequence.

interaction.prompt: A stranger walks past a person having a heart attack on the pavement and does nothing. On the general rule alone, has the stranger committed a criminal offence?
options: No — there is no general duty to rescue a stranger
Yes — failing to help is itself an offence
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Harsh as it feels, the general rule is genuinely general: no relationship, no duty, no offence.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not on the general rule — that's exactly the instinct this lesson is going to test. Keep the six exceptions in mind as you read on; without one of them, a bystander walks away clean.

parts.heading: The six doors into liability
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: 'No liability for omissions' is the headline, not the whole story. Six recognised situations convert a pure omission into a legal duty to act. Miss one of these in an exam and you'll answer the wrong question entirely — you'll be arguing about whether the defendant caused harm, when the live issue is whether they owed a duty at all.
Learn these as a checklist, not a list to recognise on sight. In application questions the facts will rarely announce 'this is a statutory duty' — you're expected to spot which door, if any, applies.

components.label: The six duty situations
points: Statutory duty — a duty created directly by Act of Parliament (e.g. failing to provide a breath specimen)
Contractual duty — a duty owed because of a job or role, even to third parties who never contracted with you
Duty from a special relationship — parent and child, or other close family relationships of dependency
Voluntary assumption of care — once you start looking after someone, the law holds you to it (Stone and Dobinson)
Duty from creating a dangerous situation — if your own act (even an innocent one) creates a risk, you must act to avert it (Miller)
Duty of a public official — certain office-holders (e.g. police officers) owe duties by virtue of their role

components.factsShort: A vulnerable couple took in the man's sister, who had anorexia. They tried, incompetently, to care for her; she died.
components.ratioShort: Voluntarily starting to care for someone creates a duty to keep caring, or to get help — incompetence at the task is not a defence to abandoning it.

expanded.facts: Stanley Stone and his partner Gwendolyn Dobinson took Stone's sister Fanny into their home. Fanny suffered from anorexia nervosa and became increasingly ill, bedridden and unable to care for herself. Stone and Dobinson, who were themselves described as ill-equipped to cope — of low intelligence, and Dobinson herself in poor health — made some efforts to help (attempting to wash her, calling a doctor once) but never got her proper medical help as she deteriorated. She died in squalid conditions.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that once the defendants had assumed responsibility for Fanny's welfare — by taking her in and making some attempt to care for her — they came under a legal duty to continue that care or summon assistance. The duty did not depend on any contract or family obligation; it arose from the voluntary undertaking itself, however badly performed.
expanded.significance: This is the leading authority for the proposition that a duty of care in criminal law can arise purely from conduct — starting to help someone who depends on you. It also confirms that being bad at the job you've taken on is irrelevant: the duty is to act reasonably or get help, not to succeed.

interaction.prompt: Put these in the order the Stone and Dobinson facts happened.
items: The couple attempt some care (washing her, one doctor visit)
Fanny's condition deteriorates without further help
Fanny dies; the couple are convicted of manslaughter
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That sequence is the whole case: the duty attaches at the point of assumption (step 1–2), and liability follows from what happens after — not from how the care started.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — the duty in this case is triggered by taking Fanny in and attempting care, before anything goes wrong. What happens afterwards is what the couple are judged on.

parts.heading: When your own act creates the danger
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: James Miller was squatting in a house. He fell asleep on a mattress with a lit cigarette in his hand. He woke to find the mattress smouldering — and instead of putting it out, he simply got up and went to sleep in another room. The house caught fire.

Miller hadn't started the fire on purpose — falling asleep with a cigarette isn't a criminal act in itself. But the House of Lords held that once he became aware his own conduct had created a danger, a duty arose to take reasonable steps to counteract it. Walking away wasn't a pure omission at all: it was a continuation of a situation he had created and could have stopped.

This is the doctrine that most often catches students out, because it doesn't look like an 'omission' case on first read — it looks like a story about a fire. The examiner's fact pattern will usually hide the duty inside a sequence of events: something goes wrong by accident, the defendant notices, and does nothing. That's Miller, every time.

components.text: A person who without lawful excuse destroys or damages any property belonging to another intending to destroy or damage any such property or being reckless as to whether any such property would be destroyed or damaged shall be guilty of an offence.
elements: Intention or recklessness as to the damage

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that triggers a Miller-style duty to act.
interaction.scenarioText: Priya is decorating a room and knocks over a candle onto a curtain without noticing. Ten minutes later she walks back in, sees the curtain smouldering, and simply closes the door and leaves the house to avoid being blamed.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the moment. Knocking the candle over was accidental and not itself culpable — the duty bites the instant Priya becomes aware of the danger she created and chooses not to act on it.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at when Priya becomes aware of the risk, rather than when she caused it. Miller turns on knowledge plus inaction, not on the original accident.

parts.heading: Life support, and where 'act' and 'omission' get slippery
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the dilemma before resolving it
body: Here's a genuinely hard question before we answer it: if a doctor switches off a ventilator keeping a patient alive, is that an act that causes death, or an omission to continue treatment? The distinction matters enormously — an act causing death raises the spectre of murder; a lawful omission does not.

The House of Lords answered this in the case of Tony Bland, who suffered catastrophic brain injury in the Hillsborough disaster and was left in a persistent vegetative state. His doctors sought permission to withdraw artificial feeding and hydration.

The court held that withdrawing treatment is properly classified as an **omission** — a decision not to continue a course of treatment — even though it involves a physical act (turning something off). Once continued treatment is no longer in the patient's best interests, there is no duty to continue it, and withdrawal is lawful.

Notice what this case is really doing: it shows that 'act' and 'omission' are not always obvious from watching what a person's hands do. The law classifies conduct by its legal character — the continuation or discontinuation of a duty — not by whether a muscle moved.

components.title: Act or omission? A decision path
components.description: A flowchart used to classify conduct as act or omission for duty purposes.

nodes.label: Does the conduct involve stopping something the defendant was already doing under a duty (e.g. treatment, care)?
Yes → likely an omission (discontinuing a duty)
No → did the defendant's own prior conduct create the danger?
Yes → Miller duty: omission to counteract a danger you created
No → check the other five duty categories (statutory, contractual, relationship, assumption of care, public office)
No duty found → pure omission, no liability

components.textAlternative: To classify conduct: first ask if the defendant is stopping something already being done under a duty (like withdrawing treatment) — if so, it's an omission. If not, ask if the defendant's own prior conduct created the danger — if so, a Miller duty to counteract it arises. If neither applies, check the remaining five duty categories (statutory, contractual, special relationship, voluntary assumption of care, public office). If none apply, this is a pure omission and there is no liability.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that withdrawing life support is legally classified as an omission rather than an act?
interaction.explanation: Bland settled this: withdrawal of treatment, however active the physical step, is treated in law as an omission — the discontinuation of a duty that is no longer owed once continued treatment is against the patient's best interests.

parts.heading: Extending Miller: duties between people who share a home
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap the tests will probe
body: One more case earns its place here because it's the one examiners return to most often: R v Evans. Gemma Evans supplied heroin to her half-sister, who then overdosed. Evans realised something was badly wrong, but — afraid of the consequences — did not call for help. Her sister died.

The Court of Appeal extended Miller beyond emergencies you cause by pure accident: Evans had supplied the drug, and once she appreciated her sister was in danger as a result, a duty arose to take reasonable steps — which, at minimum, meant seeking medical assistance. Fear of getting into trouble is not a defence to breaching that duty.

Evans matters because it shows the Miller principle isn't frozen to fires and property damage. It applies wherever a person's own conduct — even conduct that felt ordinary, like handing something to a family member — sets a chain of danger in motion that they then recognise and ignore.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often say Evans owed no duty because supplying drugs to a consenting adult 'isn't the same as' creating a dangerous situation the way starting a fire is.
components.whyItsWrong: The Miller principle doesn't require the initial conduct to be inherently dangerous or unlawful on its own — it requires that the defendant's conduct in fact created a risk, and that the defendant became aware of that risk. Supplying the drug set the chain in motion; recognising the overdose and failing to act on it is what breaches the duty.

interaction.prompt: Two scenarios. In which does an Evans-style duty most clearly arise?
interaction.scenarioA: Tom lends his car to a friend, who crashes it through no fault of Tom's, while Tom is elsewhere and unaware.
interaction.scenarioB: Tom gives his friend a prescription-strength painkiller at a party; the friend later starts choking on vomit in front of Tom, who is too drunk to want to deal with it and goes to bed.
interaction.explanation: In B, Tom's own act (supplying the pill) contributed to a chain of danger, and — critically — Tom becomes aware his friend is in danger and chooses inaction. In A, Tom has no awareness of any danger at the relevant time, so no duty is triggered on these facts.

testPool.prompt: Name the general rule governing liability for a failure to act in English criminal law.
testPool.modelAnswer: There is no liability for a pure omission — a failure to act by someone under no recognised legal duty — however serious the consequences.

testPool.prompt: Which case established that voluntarily beginning to care for someone can create a legal duty to continue?
options: R v Stone and Dobinson
R v Miller

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the six recognised duty situations?
options: Statutory duty
Contractual duty
Duty arising from being the only witness to an emergency
Duty from voluntary assumption of care
testPool.trapExplanation: Merely witnessing an emergency, with no other relationship to the victim, never creates a duty on its own — this is the core of the 'no duty to rescue' rule that this whole lesson exists to qualify.

testPool.prompt: Order the reasoning steps a court follows when deciding if withdrawing medical treatment is unlawful.
items: Classify the withdrawal as an act or an omission
If an omission, ask whether a duty to continue treatment still exists
Assess whether continued treatment is in the patient's best interests
If not in the patient's best interests, no duty to continue — withdrawal is lawful

testPool.prompt: A statutory duty to act (e.g. under road traffic legislation) differs from a Miller duty in one key respect. Which?
options: A statutory duty exists regardless of anything the defendant does or notices; a Miller duty depends on the defendant's own prior conduct and awareness
A statutory duty only applies to police officers
A Miller duty can never lead to a criminal conviction

testPool.prompt: In the passage below from R v Evans, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
testPool.passage: The defendant had supplied the drug which her sister then used. Once she appreciated, or ought reasonably to have appreciated, that her sister's condition was serious, she came under a duty to take reasonable steps to prevent the danger she had helped create. That she was afraid to call for help does not excuse the breach.
testPool.ratioSentence: Once she appreciated, or ought reasonably to have appreciated, that her sister's condition was serious, she came under a duty to take reasonable steps to prevent the danger she had helped create.

testPool.prompt: Dev is a qualified lifeguard on his day off, sunbathing at a public (unsupervised) beach. He sees a swimmer struggling but does not intervene. Does Dev owe a duty to act?
options: Yes — his professional qualification alone creates a duty wherever he happens to be
No — off duty and not employed to supervise this beach, he is in the same position as any other bystander
Yes — because he is the most qualified person present
testPool.explanation: A contractual or professional duty attaches to the role being performed, not the qualification itself. Off-duty and unemployed for the purpose, Dev is a pure bystander — however well placed he is to help.

testPool.prompt: Sam is babysitting his young niece under an informal family arrangement. She swallows something and starts choking. Sam panics and does nothing, hoping it resolves itself. Which duty situation applies?
options: Voluntary assumption of care
Statutory duty
No duty — informal arrangements never count
testPool.explanation: Taking on the care of a child, even informally and without payment, is a textbook voluntary assumption of care — Stone and Dobinson's principle, not a contract.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that converts this from a pure omission into a Miller-style duty.
testPool.scenarioText: Leah accidentally leaves a space heater too close to a pile of laundry when she goes out. She returns, smells burning, checks the room, and sees the laundry has started to smoulder — then decides to ignore it and watch television instead.
tappableSpans: leaves a space heater too close
testPool.explanation: Awareness is the trigger. Leaving the heater too close was careless but not itself the duty-creating moment; the duty attaches once Leah becomes aware of the danger she created.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario most closely mirrors the reasoning in R v Miller, rather than R v Stone and Dobinson?
testPool.scenarioA: A landlord notices their elderly, isolated tenant hasn't been seen in days and does nothing, having no duty of care under the tenancy.
testPool.scenarioB: A camper accidentally knocks over a lantern near dry brush, notices the small fire starting, and walks away rather than stamping it out.
testPool.explanation: B is Miller: an accidental act creates a danger, the defendant becomes aware, and fails to counteract it. A involves no prior assumption of care and no conduct by the landlord creating the risk, so no duty arises on these facts at all.

testPool.prompt: A nurse on shift ignores a patient's call bell for two hours out of laziness, and the patient's condition worsens. Is the nurse under a duty to act?
options: Yes — contractual/professional duty from her employed role
No — nurses only owe duties to patients they are formally assigned to

testPool.prompt: Marcus is fixing a gas appliance as an unqualified favour to his elderly neighbour. He realises partway through that he has made the connection unsafe, but decides finishing quickly is easier than admitting the mistake and calling a professional. The neighbour is later hospitalised from a gas leak. Analyse whether Marcus owed a duty to act.
factsToOrder: Marcus is unqualified to do the repair
Marcus is acting as a favour, with no contract
Marcus realises the connection is unsafe partway through
Marcus chooses to finish rather than stop and get help

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Marcus owed a legal duty to act once he realised the gas connection was unsafe.
modelAnswer.rule: A duty to act arises where a defendant's own conduct creates a dangerous situation and the defendant becomes aware of that danger (Miller); the absence of a contract or qualification does not prevent a duty arising from voluntary conduct.
modelAnswer.application: Marcus's own act (the unsafe repair) created the danger. He does not need a contract or qualification for a Miller duty to bite — what matters is that his conduct created the risk and he became aware of it partway through. His choice to finish rather than stop and get help is a failure to take the reasonable steps the duty requires.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Marcus owed a duty to act once he recognised the danger; his failure to stop or seek help breaches it.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best explains why Bland classified withdrawal of treatment as an omission rather than an act?
options: Because doctors are never held criminally liable for treatment decisions
Because the legal character of conduct depends on whether a duty is being discontinued, not on the physical movements involved
Because the patient had consented in advance to withdrawal
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answers focus on consent or on doctors' immunity — neither is the actual reasoning. Bland turns on classifying the conduct: discontinuing a duty no longer owed is an omission, whatever physical act that involves.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating 'the defendant didn't do anything wrong at first' as the end of the analysis. It's usually the beginning: check what happened next.
